name: Bridge of No Return
scope: Whole original native six-vertex Bridge of No Return and both mapped bridge-axis halves, approximately144.68m long/4.74m wide. Low straight concrete slab/girder crossing with narrow carriageway, curbs, repeated pierced vertical-slot concrete parapets, heavier panel/end posts, concrete top rails, four light-blue cylindrical south/east entry bollards, integral low abutments and bounded partly concealed supporting bents. Exclude checkpoint buildings, MDL sign, adjacent roads, trees, people, vehicles, river water, full border plaza/site floor and other nearby bridges.
era: Surviving concrete bridge represented from published2008 Army entry photograph with four blue bollards; published1975/1976 creator-released photographs provide auxiliary whole-bridge/parapet form. Hidden supports/heights and exact present-day weathering remain estimates; independent historical checkpoints are excluded.

references.filename: The Bridge of No Return, CP-3 Dec 75a.jpg
references.caption: I took this picture in December of 1975, from the same location the picture of the Axe Murder Incident were taken from 8 months later. At the closest end of the Bridge of No Return is CP#3, "The Lonliest Outpost in the World". At the furthest end of the bridge is North Korean territory, outside of the JSA. Notice the 2 1/2 ton truck sitting at CP#3. The two people who would work there during daylight hours needed a big, heavy truck to break through the road barriers the North Koreans had erected for the occasions when they tried to block the road. Also visible in the picture is the tree the fight was over. In summertime, the tree was twice as full as it appears in this picture, basically obscuring visibility between UNC posts. Since the North Koreans would try to kidnap the people working at CP#3 and drag them across the bridge, maintaining visibility between the checkpoints was imperative for their safety during the summer months.
references.sourceFamily: commons:The Bridge of No Return, CP-3 Dec 75a.jpg

references.caption: I took this picture in March of 1976. Across the bridge is KPA#4. One of the three KPA guards assigned at the checkpoint is visible in the window. Looking closely, you can see a red and white barrier across the road next to the checkpoint.
